requirements.title: Intended purpose and use boundaries
requirements.interpretation: The intended purpose, users, affected persons, operating context, expected outputs, permitted uses, prohibited uses and foreseeable misuse are precise enough to govern design and evaluation.

requirements.title: AI suitability, proportionality and value hypothesis
requirements.interpretation: The organization demonstrates that AI is a proportionate mechanism for a defined problem and that expected value is measurable against cost, alternatives and risk.

requirements.title: Value-chain roles and responsibility boundaries
requirements.interpretation: Organizational, contractual and regulatory roles across the complete AI value chain are identified and matched to real control and accountability.

requirements.title: Risk, legal and regulatory classification
requirements.interpretation: The complete system and actual use are classified through a reviewable applicability analysis covering role, risk, jurisdiction, data, impact and sector obligations.

requirements.title: Lifecycle stage and transition boundary
requirements.interpretation: The current stage, permitted activities, target stage, acceptance criteria and authorization boundary are explicit from qualification through retirement.

requirements.title: Data inventory, provenance and lineage
requirements.interpretation: Training, tuning, retrieval, prompt, evaluation, operational and output data are separately identifiable from origin through transformation, storage, transfer and deletion.

requirements.title: Purpose limitation and data minimization
requirements.interpretation: Only data demonstrably necessary and proportionate for the declared purpose and lifecycle stage are processed and retained.

requirements.title: Privacy and data-subject governance
requirements.interpretation: Personal-data processing, lawful basis, transparency, rights, privacy risks and impact-assessment duties are operationalized in the system and its lifecycle.

requirements.title: Confidentiality and information-boundary control
requirements.interpretation: Confidential, restricted, customer-controlled and security-sensitive information remains within approved identity, tenant, provider, logging and contractual boundaries.

requirements.title: Intellectual property, licensing and content rights
requirements.interpretation: The organization has a defensible and traceable basis to use, transform, train on, retrieve, generate and distribute relevant data, models, code and outputs.

requirements.title: Model, agent and component inventory
requirements.interpretation: Models, agents, prompts, tools, APIs, datasets, providers, infrastructure, versions and owners are registered and linked to the assessed system.

requirements.title: Model and provider suitability
requirements.interpretation: Model and provider selections are evidence-based for task quality, language, latency, security, privacy, resilience, cost, contract and risk.

requirements.title: Agent autonomy and tool permissioning
requirements.interpretation: Agent authority is explicit, least-privilege, stage-appropriate, budgeted, observable and bounded by deterministic authorization for consequential actions.

requirements.title: Provider, vendor and contractual governance
requirements.interpretation: Third-party AI services are evaluated, contractually governed, monitored and replaceable in the context of the actual system.

requirements.title: AI supply-chain integrity and change control
requirements.interpretation: AI models, datasets, libraries, tools, services and update channels have verifiable provenance, controlled baselines and risk-based change gates.

requirements.title: Secure and isolated AI architecture
requirements.interpretation: The system uses defense in depth, explicit trust boundaries and enforced identity, network, environment, tenant, secrets and data-flow controls.

requirements.title: Functional quality, accuracy and reliability
requirements.interpretation: End-to-end performance is evaluated on representative tasks, users, contexts and failure modes against consequence-based acceptance thresholds.

requirements.title: AI-specific security and adversarial resilience
requirements.interpretation: The system identifies and controls attack paths that exploit AI models, prompts, training or retrieval data, generated outputs, tools and feedback loops, and verifies resilience through representative adversarial testing and monitoring.

requirements.title: Traceability, reproducibility and observability
requirements.interpretation: Material outputs and actions can be reconstructed from evidence, data, component versions, prompts, tools, validations and human decisions with sufficient operational telemetry.

requirements.title: Safety, failure handling and recovery
requirements.interpretation: Foreseeable unsafe states are constrained through fail-safe behavior, interruption, fallback, rollback, human takeover, incident response and recovery testing.

requirements.title: Human and fundamental-rights impact
requirements.interpretation: The organization evaluates direct, indirect and cumulative benefits and harms for users, non-users, affected groups and rights across the actual context.

requirements.title: Fairness and non-discrimination
requirements.interpretation: Contextual fairness objectives, relevant groups, data and decision pathways are defined, measured and governed for unacceptable disparity.

requirements.title: Transparency and communication
requirements.interpretation: Users and affected persons receive timely, accurate and actionable information about AI use, purpose, limitations, data use, human involvement and relevant consequences.

requirements.title: Meaningful human oversight
requirements.interpretation: Competent humans have sufficient information, authority, time and technical ability to review, intervene, override and escalate at material decision points.

requirements.title: Contestability, correction, accessibility and AI literacy
requirements.interpretation: Material outcomes can be questioned and corrected through accessible human recourse, while users, reviewers and decision-makers have role-appropriate competence.

requirements.title: Ownership and accountable operating model
requirements.interpretation: One accountable system owner and clearly assigned business, technical, data, model, security, privacy, operations and decision roles exercise authority throughout the lifecycle.

requirements.title: Compliance evidence and documentation integrity
requirements.interpretation: Material claims, requirements, controls and readiness conclusions are linked to current, scoped, attributable and sufficient evidence that matches implementation and operation.

requirements.title: Risk, control and residual-risk management
requirements.interpretation: System-specific risks are linked to controls, evidence, owners, treatment criteria, residual uncertainty and authorized acceptance.

requirements.title: Decision rights, authorization and escalation
requirements.interpretation: The correct human authority makes timely, proportional and recorded lifecycle decisions, clearly separated from automated recommendations.

requirements.title: Monitoring, incidents, change, re-evaluation and retirement
requirements.interpretation: Quality, risk, security, impact and compliance are monitored; incidents and material changes trigger response, reassessment, reauthorization or controlled retirement.

controls.title: Intended purpose and use boundaries

questions.question: Is the intended purpose and decision context specific, bounded and testable?
Are purpose and use boundaries implemented consistently in workflows, data use, access and product behavior?
Does current evidence show that actual and foreseeable use remains within the declared boundary?

indicators: Purpose reflected in architecture and evaluations
controls.definition: The intended purpose, users, affected persons, operating context, expected outputs, permitted uses, prohibited uses and foreseeable misuse are precise enough to govern design and evaluation.

controls.title: AI suitability, proportionality and value hypothesis

questions.question: Is the problem, desired outcome and measurable value hypothesis defined independently of the AI solution?
Has the chosen AI approach been compared with simpler alternatives and implemented with explicit cost-risk trade-offs?
Do representative trials show sufficient value and feasibility to justify progression, with stop criteria applied?

indicators: Value metrics and owners are named
Cost and operational consequences are considered
Continuation and stop criteria are enforced
controls.definition: The organization demonstrates that AI is a proportionate mechanism for a defined problem and that expected value is measurable against cost, alternatives and risk.

controls.title: Value-chain roles and responsibility boundaries

questions.question: Are system, business, provider, deployer, integrator and component roles explicitly determined?
Are responsibilities implemented through contracts, operating procedures, access and ownership assignments?
Does evidence show that each party can and does discharge the responsibilities assigned to it?

indicators: System and business owners are named
Provider and deployer duties are separated
controls.definition: Organizational, contractual and regulatory roles across the complete AI value chain are identified and matched to real control and accountability.

controls.title: Risk, legal and regulatory classification

questions.question: Are applicable jurisdictions, roles, prohibited-practice screens, risk classes and adjacent legal regimes identified from actual use?
Are classification outcomes implemented as controls, documentation duties, review routes and transition constraints?
Is the rationale current, evidence-backed, independently reviewed where needed and linked to reclassification triggers?

controls.definition: The complete system and actual use are classified through a reviewable applicability analysis covering role, risk, jurisdiction, data, impact and sector obligations.

controls.title: Lifecycle stage and transition boundary

questions.question: Are current and target lifecycle stages, scope and permitted activities explicitly defined?
Are environment, data, access and user boundaries technically and operationally enforced for the current stage?
Does evidence demonstrate that transition criteria are met and the correct authority has approved progression?

controls.definition: The current stage, permitted activities, target stage, acceptance criteria and authorization boundary are explicit from qualification through retirement.

controls.title: Data inventory, provenance and lineage

questions.question: Are material data classes, sources, owners, destinations and uses inventoried with stable identifiers?
Are lineage, transformation, quality, licensing and transfer controls implemented across the actual data flow?
Can representative outputs and decisions be traced to current, authorized and sufficiently reliable data evidence?

controls.definition: Training, tuning, retrieval, prompt, evaluation, operational and output data are separately identifiable from origin through transformation, storage, transfer and deletion.

controls.title: Purpose limitation and data minimization

questions.question: Is necessity defined for each material data category, field and retention period?
Are minimization, abstraction, tokenization, synthetic-data and deletion controls implemented in every relevant store and interface?
Do tests and operational evidence show that unnecessary content is excluded and deletion or scope changes propagate?

controls.definition: Only data demonstrably necessary and proportionate for the declared purpose and lifecycle stage are processed and retained.

controls.title: Privacy and data-subject governance

questions.question: Are personal-data categories, purposes, lawful basis, rights and impact-assessment triggers determined?
Are privacy requirements implemented across architecture, access, logging, retention, providers and user workflows?
Do tests and operational records demonstrate rights fulfilment, deletion, restriction and privacy-control effectiveness?

indicators: Rights can be fulfilled end to end
controls.definition: Personal-data processing, lawful basis, transparency, rights, privacy risks and impact-assessment duties are operationalized in the system and its lifecycle.

controls.title: Confidentiality and information-boundary control

questions.question: Are information classes, confidentiality obligations and prohibited disclosure paths explicitly defined?
Are secrets isolation, least privilege, tenant separation, provider settings and leakage controls technically enforced?
Do leakage, cross-tenant, unauthorized reuse and output-disclosure tests demonstrate effective boundaries?

indicators: Secrets are excluded from model-visible context
Provider retention and training settings are known
controls.definition: Confidential, restricted, customer-controlled and security-sensitive information remains within approved identity, tenant, provider, logging and contractual boundaries.

controls.title: Intellectual property, licensing and content rights

questions.question: Are rights, licences, restrictions, attribution and ownership conditions identified for all material assets and outputs?
Are those conditions implemented in ingestion, training, retrieval, generation, review and distribution workflows?

controls.definition: The organization has a defensible and traceable basis to use, transform, train on, retrieve, generate and distribute relevant data, models, code and outputs.

controls.title: Model, agent and component inventory

questions.question: Are all material AI and supporting components, versions, configurations, owners and roles inventoried?

controls.definition: Models, agents, prompts, tools, APIs, datasets, providers, infrastructure, versions and owners are registered and linked to the assessed system.

controls.title: Model and provider suitability

controls.definition: Model and provider selections are evidence-based for task quality, language, latency, security, privacy, resilience, cost, contract and risk.
